strings.hub.holy_see.title: The Holy See
strings.hub.holy_see.subtitle: Everything about the Vatican
strings.hub.holy_see.intro: The smallest sovereign state on earth, the tomb of an apostle, a chapel that elects popes, and a government that predates almost every nation it speaks to. Start anywhere.

strings.fact.vatican_city.title: The Vatican in numbers
strings.fact.vatican_city.area.label: Area
strings.fact.vatican_city.area.value: 44 hectares (0.44 km²) — the smallest sovereign state in the world
strings.fact.vatican_city.population.label: Residents

strings.fact.vatican_city.founded.label: Founded

strings.fact.vatican_city.currency.label: Currency

strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.title: The Holy See and Vatican City are not the same thing
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.lead: One is a government. The other is the plot of land that keeps it independent. Almost every news report confuses them.
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.p1: When an ambassador is accredited, when a treaty is signed, when the Church speaks at the United Nations, the party involved is the Holy See — not Vatican City. The distinction is not pedantry: they are two different subjects with two different legal characters.
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.p2: The Holy See is the episcopal see of Rome: the Pope together with the offices that assist him in governing the universal Church. It has existed for as long as there have been bishops of Rome, and it exercised international personality for centuries before it had any modern territory at all.
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.grid.see.label: The Holy See
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.grid.see.value: The governing authority of the Catholic Church. Sends and receives ambassadors, signs concordats, sits as a permanent observer at the UN.
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.grid.state.label: Vatican City State
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.grid.state.value: A 44-hectare territory created in 1929 for one purpose: to guarantee that the Holy See answers to no other government.
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.p3: The relationship runs one way. The Holy See governs the State; the State exists to serve the Holy See's independence. If the territory disappeared tomorrow, the Holy See would continue — as it did between 1870 and 1929, when it had no territory and still maintained diplomatic relations.
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.callout.title: A useful test
strings.art.holy_see_vs_state.callout.body: Diplomacy, doctrine and Church governance belong to the Holy See. Passports, stamps, the pharmacy and the railway belong to the State.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.title: The Lateran Treaty
strings.art.lateran_treaty.lead: For fifty-nine years the popes refused to leave the Vatican. In 1929 a treaty ended the standoff and drew a border around it.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.p1: On 11 February 1929, Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri and Benito Mussolini, acting for King Victor Emmanuel III, signed three documents in the Lateran Palace: a treaty creating Vatican City, a financial convention settling compensation for the lost Papal States, and a concordat regulating the Church's position in Italy.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.p2: Italian troops entered Rome through the breach at Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, ending the Papal States. [[pope:pius_ix|Pius IX]] refused to recognise the annexation and withdrew inside the Vatican walls. He and his four successors never left them — the so-called prisoners in the Vatican.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.p3: Italy tried to settle the matter unilaterally with the Law of Guarantees in 1871, offering the Pope personal privileges and an annual payment. Every pope refused it: a right granted by Italian statute could be withdrawn by Italian statute, and that is precisely what sovereignty is not.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.li1: Created Vatican City State and recognised the Holy See's full sovereignty over it.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.li2: Ended the Roman Question: the Holy See recognised the Kingdom of Italy with Rome as its capital.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.li3: Granted extraterritorial status to properties outside the walls — the major basilicas, Castel Gandolfo, and several curial buildings.
strings.art.lateran_treaty.li4: Settled financial compensation for the territory lost in 1870.
strings.art.how_it_runs.title: How the Vatican actually runs
strings.art.how_it_runs.lead: An absolute elective monarchy with a fire brigade, a supermarket, and one of the world's oldest civil services.
strings.art.how_it_runs.p1: The Pope holds legislative, executive and judicial power over the State. In practice he delegates day-to-day governance to the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, whose president heads the Governorate — the body that runs the museums, the post office, the health service, the gardens and the police.
strings.art.how_it_runs.p2: Distinct from the Governorate is the Roman Curia, which assists the Pope in governing the universal Church rather than the territory. Its structure was reorganised by the apostolic constitution Praedicate Evangelium in 2022, which put evangelisation first and opened curial leadership to lay men and women.
strings.art.how_it_runs.li_secretariat: The Secretariat of State — the Pope's closest office, handling general affairs and diplomatic relations.
strings.art.how_it_runs.li_dicasteries: The dicasteries — sixteen departments covering evangelisation, doctrine, charity, the sacraments, saints' causes, clergy, laity, Eastern Churches and more.
strings.art.how_it_runs.li_tribunals: The tribunals — the Apostolic Penitentiary, the Apostolic Signatura, and the Roman Rota, which hears marriage nullity appeals.
strings.art.how_it_runs.li_economy: The economic bodies — the Secretariat for the Economy, APSA, the Council for the Economy and the Auditor General.
strings.art.how_it_runs.p3: Behind the basilica the State functions like a very small town: a heliport, a railway station, a pharmacy known for stocking medicines unavailable in Italy, a supermarket, a printing press, the Vatican Observatory, and the newspaper L'Osservatore Romano. Most of the people who work here live in Rome and commute through the gates each morning.
strings.art.sistine_history.title: The Sistine Chapel: a history
strings.art.sistine_history.lead: It was built as a fortified chapel for the papal court. Two commissions turned it into the most visited room on earth.
strings.art.sistine_history.p1: The chapel was raised between 1473 and 1481 for [[pope:sixtus_iv|Sixtus IV]], who gave it his name. Its proportions — roughly 40.9 metres long, 13.4 wide and 20.7 high — are traditionally said to follow the dimensions of the Temple of Solomon as given in the First Book of Kings. The walls were built thick and the windows set high: this was a chapel that could be defended.
strings.art.sistine_history.p2: In 1481–82 Sixtus summoned the best painters in Italy. Perugino, Botticelli, Ghirlandaio, Cosimo Rosselli and their workshops covered the side walls with two parallel cycles: the life of Moses facing the life of Christ, law answering grace, panel for panel. Visitors walk straight past them on the way to the ceiling.
strings.art.sistine_history.card_ghirlandaio: Ghirlandaio — The Calling of the Apostles
strings.art.sistine_history.p3: [[pope:julius_ii|Julius II]] wanted the ceiling repainted. Michelangelo, who considered himself a sculptor and was then at work on the Pope's tomb, resisted the commission and took it anyway. He worked for four years on scaffolding of his own design, standing rather than lying down, and the original plan of twelve apostles grew into more than three hundred figures.
strings.art.sistine_history.p4: The ceiling was unveiled on 31 October 1512. Its nine central panels run from the first act of creation above the altar to the drunkenness of Noah above the entrance — the story of the world before the Law, painted above a chapel where the Law and the Gospel already faced each other on the walls.
strings.art.sistine_history.p5: Nearly a quarter of a century later Michelangelo returned, now in his sixties, to paint the altar wall. The Last Judgement was commissioned by Clement VII and carried out under Paul III. Its unclothed figures were controversial from the start; after the Council of Trent, Daniele da Volterra was tasked with adding drapery, earning him the nickname il Braghettone — the breeches-maker.
strings.art.sistine_history.p6: Between 1980 and 1999 the frescoes were cleaned of centuries of candle soot and animal glue. The colours that emerged were so much brighter than expected that some art historians argued the restorers had stripped away Michelangelo's finishing touches. The debate has cooled, but it has never entirely ended.
strings.art.sistine_layout.title: Reading the ceiling
strings.art.sistine_layout.lead: Everyone looks up and sees the Creation of Adam. Here is what surrounds it, and in what order to read it.
strings.art.sistine_layout.p1: The ceiling is a painted architecture: a fictive framework of ribs and thrones inside which every figure has a place. Once you can see the frame, the whole scheme organises itself in a few seconds.
strings.art.sistine_layout.p2: Work from the centre outwards and downwards. The narrative runs from the altar towards the entrance — which means that if you walk in and read forwards, you are reading the story backwards.
strings.art.sistine_layout.li_genesis: Nine central panels from Genesis, alternating large and small: the three days of creation, the creation and fall of humanity, and the story of Noah.
strings.art.sistine_layout.li_prophets: Seven prophets of Israel and five pagan sibyls enthroned around the edges — the two ways the world was said to have been told that Christ was coming.
strings.art.sistine_layout.li_spandrels: Corner spandrels with four dramatic deliverances of Israel, including the bronze serpent and the death of Haman.
strings.art.sistine_layout.li_lunettes: Lunettes and severies above the windows carrying the ancestors of Christ — the genealogy from Matthew's Gospel, painted as ordinary families waiting.
strings.art.sistine_layout.callout.title: The gap in the Creation of Adam
strings.art.sistine_layout.callout.body: The fingers do not touch. Whatever else is being shown, the moment chosen is the one just before contact — the reach, not the arrival.
strings.art.sistine_layout.h_conclave: The room where popes are chosen
strings.art.sistine_layout.p3: The chapel is not a museum piece but a working liturgical space, and above all the place of the conclave. The first was held here in 1492; since 1878 every conclave has taken place beneath this ceiling. The cardinals cast their ballots in front of the Last Judgement, which is presumably the point.

strings.diag.sc.g1.label: The Separation of Light from Darkness
strings.diag.sc.g1.blurb: The first act of creation, directly above the altar.
strings.diag.sc.g2.label: The Creation of the Sun, Moon and Plants
strings.diag.sc.g2.blurb: God appears twice in one panel, sweeping through in opposite directions.
strings.diag.sc.g3.label: The Separation of Land from Water
strings.diag.sc.g3.blurb: The waters gathered, and dry land appearing beneath them.
strings.diag.sc.g4.label: The Creation of Adam
strings.diag.sc.g4.blurb: The most reproduced image in Western art. The fingers never meet.
strings.diag.sc.g5.label: The Creation of Eve
strings.diag.sc.g5.blurb: The exact centre of the ceiling, and the hinge of the whole narrative.
strings.diag.sc.g6.label: The Fall and the Expulsion
strings.diag.sc.g6.blurb: Two moments in one frame, divided by the tree and the angel's sword.
strings.diag.sc.g7.label: The Sacrifice of Noah
strings.diag.sc.g7.blurb: Painted before the Flood panel, though it comes after it in Genesis.
strings.diag.sc.g8.label: The Flood
strings.diag.sc.g8.blurb: The first panel Michelangelo painted — and the one that taught him to work larger.
strings.diag.sc.g9.label: The Drunkenness of Noah
strings.diag.sc.g9.blurb: The story ends above the door: humanity fallen again, this time on its own.
strings.diag.sc.jonah.label: The Prophet Jonah
strings.diag.sc.jonah.blurb: Above the altar, thrown backwards — three days in the fish, read as a sign of the Resurrection.
strings.diag.sc.jeremiah.label: The Prophet Jeremiah
strings.diag.sc.jeremiah.blurb: Silent, head in hand. Often taken as Michelangelo's self-portrait in mood if not in feature.
strings.diag.sc.libyan.label: The Libyan Sibyl
strings.diag.sc.libyan.blurb: Caught mid-turn, closing her book — the most athletic figure on the ceiling.
strings.diag.sc.persian.label: The Persian Sibyl
strings.diag.sc.persian.blurb: Aged and short-sighted, holding her book close to her face.
strings.diag.sc.daniel.label: The Prophet Daniel
strings.diag.sc.daniel.blurb: Writing at speed, a volume held open below him by a small assistant.
strings.diag.sc.ezekiel.label: The Prophet Ezekiel
strings.diag.sc.ezekiel.blurb: Twisting round mid-argument, scroll gripped in one hand.
strings.diag.sc.cumaean.label: The Cumaean Sibyl
strings.diag.sc.cumaean.blurb: Massively built, the prophetess Virgil placed at the gates of the underworld.
strings.diag.sc.erythraean.label: The Erythraean Sibyl
strings.diag.sc.erythraean.blurb: Turning a page while a boy lights her lamp behind her.
strings.diag.sc.isaiah.label: The Prophet Isaiah
strings.diag.sc.isaiah.blurb: Interrupted in his reading by the child at his shoulder.
strings.diag.sc.joel.label: The Prophet Joel
strings.diag.sc.joel.blurb: Unrolling a scroll with both hands, absorbed in it.
strings.diag.sc.delphic.label: The Delphic Sibyl
strings.diag.sc.delphic.blurb: Young and startled, looking out past the viewer — among the first figures painted.
strings.diag.sc.zechariah.label: The Prophet Zechariah
strings.diag.sc.zechariah.blurb: Above the entrance, searching a book. The first figure most visitors walk under without seeing.
strings.tl.roman_question.title: The Roman Question, 1870–1984
strings.tl.rq.1870.title: Porta Pia
strings.tl.rq.1870.body: Italian troops breach the walls on 20 September. The Papal States end; Rome becomes the capital of Italy.
strings.tl.rq.1871.title: The Law of Guarantees
strings.tl.rq.1871.body: Italy unilaterally offers the Pope privileges and an annual payment. Pius IX refuses, and no successor accepts.
strings.tl.rq.1929.title: The Lateran Treaty
strings.tl.rq.1929.body: Vatican City State is created and the Holy See recognises the Kingdom of Italy. The standoff ends after fifty-nine years.
strings.tl.rq.1984.title: The revised concordat
strings.tl.rq.1984.body: The Villa Madama agreement revises the 1929 concordat and ends Catholicism's status as the state religion of Italy.
strings.tl.sistine.title: The Sistine Chapel, 1473–1999
strings.tl.sc.1473.title: Construction under Sixtus IV
strings.tl.sc.1473.body: A new papal chapel replaces the medieval Cappella Magna, built to be defensible.
strings.tl.sc.1481.title: The wall cycles
strings.tl.sc.1481.body: Perugino, Botticelli, Ghirlandaio and Rosselli paint the lives of Moses and of Christ on facing walls.
strings.tl.sc.1492.title: The first conclave held here
strings.tl.sc.1492.body: The chapel hosts a papal election for the first time. It becomes the permanent venue from 1878 onwards.
strings.tl.sc.1508.title: Michelangelo paints the ceiling
strings.tl.sc.1508.body: Four years of work for Julius II, unveiled on 31 October 1512.
strings.tl.sc.1536.title: The Last Judgement
strings.tl.sc.1536.body: Michelangelo returns to paint the altar wall, commissioned by Clement VII and completed under Paul III.
strings.tl.sc.1564.title: The drapery added
strings.tl.sc.1564.body: After the Council of Trent, Daniele da Volterra covers parts of the Last Judgement — hence il Braghettone.
strings.tl.sc.1980.title: The great restoration
strings.tl.sc.1980.body: Nineteen years of cleaning reveal colours so vivid that the restoration itself becomes a controversy.
strings.art.st_peters.title: History and Construction
strings.art.st_peters.lead: From a modest shrine over the apostle's grave to the largest church in Christendom.
strings.art.st_peters.p1: Constantine ordered the first basilica over the traditional site of St. Peter's tomb in the fourth century. By the Renaissance, the aging building could no longer hold the weight of its own history, and in 1506 Pope Julius II laid the foundation stone for an entirely new church.
strings.art.st_peters.p2: The rebuilding took more than a century and passed through the hands of several master architects, including Donato Bramante, Raphael, and Michelangelo, who designed the great dome in his final years without living to see it completed. The basilica was consecrated by Pope Urban VIII in 1626.
strings.art.st_peters.p3: Bernini's bronze baldachin rises nearly 30 metres over the papal altar, itself positioned directly above the traditional site of St. Peter's grave. The basilica can hold tens of thousands of visitors, and brass markers set into the nave floor show how the naves of other great cathedrals would fit inside it.
strings.art.st_peters.callout.title: The Pietà
strings.art.st_peters.callout.body: Michelangelo's Pietà, sculpted when he was in his early twenties, stands just inside the entrance, behind glass since a 1972 attack.
strings.art.papal_tombs.title: Where the Popes Are Buried
strings.art.papal_tombs.lead: Most rest beneath St. Peter's itself; a few chose otherwise.
strings.art.papal_tombs.p1: Tradition holds that the apostle Peter was buried on Vatican Hill after his martyrdom, and the high altar of the basilica that bears his name stands directly above the site excavated in the twentieth century as his tomb. Since then, the Vatican Grottoes beneath the basilica floor have become the resting place of dozens of popes.
strings.art.papal_tombs.list.peter: St. Peter, beneath the papal altar
strings.art.papal_tombs.list.jp2: John Paul II, moved to a chapel in the main basilica after his 2011 beatification
strings.art.papal_tombs.list.renaissance: Julius II and other Renaissance popes, in elaborate tomb monuments throughout the basilica
strings.art.papal_tombs.p2: Burial in St. Peter's is customary rather than required, and a handful of popes are buried elsewhere in Rome by personal choice — Pope Francis, for instance, chose the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, continuing a much older tradition of papal burials at Rome's other major basilicas.
strings.art.museums.title: The Vatican Museums
strings.art.museums.lead: One of the world's largest museum complexes, and the only way most visitors reach the Sistine Chapel.
strings.art.museums.p1: The museums trace back to a single marble statue, the Laocoön, acquired by Pope Julius II in 1506. Later popes kept adding to the collection, and today the galleries stretch for several kilometres through the Apostolic Palace.
strings.art.museums.list.raphael: The Raphael Rooms, frescoed by Raphael and his workshop for Pope Julius II
strings.art.museums.list.maps: The Gallery of Maps, lined with painted topographical maps of Italy
strings.art.museums.list.pinacoteca: The Pinacoteca, the Vatican's picture gallery of paintings from the medieval period onward
strings.art.museums.list.egyptian: Egyptian and Etruscan collections, gathered by nineteenth-century popes
strings.art.museums.p2: The standard visitor route ends at the Sistine Chapel, which functions as both the final stop on the museum tour and the site of the conclave that elects a new pope.
strings.art.canon_law.title: What Is Canon Law
strings.art.canon_law.lead: The Church's own body of law, distinct from the civil law of any state.
strings.art.canon_law.p1: Canon law governs the internal life of the Catholic Church: how sacraments are administered, how dioceses and parishes are organised, how clergy are formed and disciplined, and how marriage cases are judged in Church tribunals.
strings.art.canon_law.p2: The Latin Church follows the Code of Canon Law, promulgated by Pope John Paul II in 1983 to replace the 1917 code. The Eastern Catholic Churches, which are in full communion with Rome but keep their own liturgical and legal traditions, follow a separate Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches, issued in 1990.
strings.art.canon_law.callout.title: Not the Same as Doctrine
strings.art.canon_law.callout.body: Canon law is separate from moral theology — it governs Church structure and procedure, not primarily doctrine.
strings.art.papal_documents.title: Kinds of Papal Documents
strings.art.papal_documents.lead: Not every papal statement carries the same weight or form.
strings.art.papal_documents.p1: Popes teach and govern through several distinct kinds of written document, each with its own weight and audience.
strings.art.papal_documents.grid.encyclical.valu: A letter on doctrine or morals, usually addressed to the whole Church
strings.art.papal_documents.grid.constitution.va: The most solemn form, used for the weightiest matters of governance or doctrine
strings.art.papal_documents.grid.exhortation.val: Pastoral encouragement, often following a synod of bishops
strings.art.papal_documents.grid.motu_proprio.va: Literally "on his own initiative" — a decree the pope issues without a prior request
strings.art.papal_documents.p2: Older forms survive too: a papal bull, named for the lead seal (bulla) once attached to it, was the traditional format for the most formal documents, and is still used for acts such as canonisations.
strings.art.seeing_the_pope.title: Seeing the Pope
strings.art.seeing_the_pope.lead: Two regular occasions bring the pope before the public.
strings.art.seeing_the_pope.p1: The General Audience is held most Wednesdays, usually in St. Peter's Square or, in poor weather or winter, in the Paul VI Audience Hall. Attendance is free; tickets are arranged in advance through the Prefecture of the Papal Household.
strings.art.seeing_the_pope.p2: On Sundays at noon, the pope appears at the window of the Apostolic Palace overlooking St. Peter's Square to lead the Angelus prayer and offer a short reflection, weather and health permitting. No ticket is needed — the square is open to anyone.
strings.stepper.conclave.title: How a Conclave Works
strings.stepper.conclave.intro: The process that elects a new pope, largely unchanged since the fourteenth century.
strings.stepper.conclave.step1.title: Sede Vacante Begins
strings.stepper.conclave.step1.body: The papal see falls vacant on the pope's death or resignation. The Camerlengo formally confirms it and takes charge of Vatican administration until a new pope is elected.
strings.stepper.conclave.step2.title: General Congregations
strings.stepper.conclave.step2.body: Cardinals from around the world gather in Rome for daily meetings to discuss the needs of the Church before the conclave itself begins.
strings.stepper.conclave.step3.title: Entering the Conclave
strings.stepper.conclave.step3.body: Cardinal electors — those under 80 — process into the Sistine Chapel. The Master of Ceremonies calls "Extra omnes," and everyone else leaves; the doors are sealed.
strings.stepper.conclave.step4.title: Balloting
strings.stepper.conclave.step4.body: Cardinals vote by secret paper ballot, up to four rounds a day, until one candidate wins a two-thirds majority.
strings.stepper.conclave.step5.title: Smoke Signals
strings.stepper.conclave.step5.body: Ballots are burned after each round. Chemicals are added to colour the smoke: black means no result, white means a pope has been elected.
strings.stepper.conclave.step6.title: Habemus Papam
strings.stepper.conclave.step6.body: The senior cardinal deacon announces the new pope's name from the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, who then appears to give his first blessing.
strings.timeline.councils.title: The Ecumenical Councils
strings.timeline.councils.nicaea1.title: First Council of Nicaea
strings.timeline.councils.nicaea1.body: Defined the divinity of Christ against Arianism and produced the first form of the Nicene Creed.
strings.timeline.councils.ephesus.title: Council of Ephesus
strings.timeline.councils.ephesus.body: Affirmed Mary as Theotokos, "God-bearer," against Nestorius.
strings.timeline.councils.chalcedon.title: Council of Chalcedon
strings.timeline.councils.chalcedon.body: Defined Christ's two natures, divine and human, in one person.
strings.timeline.councils.lateran4.title: Fourth Lateran Council
strings.timeline.councils.lateran4.body: One of the largest medieval councils, reforming Church discipline and defining transubstantiation.
strings.timeline.councils.trent.title: Council of Trent
strings.timeline.councils.trent.body: The Church's response to the Protestant Reformation, reshaping doctrine, discipline, and liturgy for centuries.
strings.timeline.councils.vatican1.title: First Vatican Council
strings.timeline.councils.vatican1.body: Defined papal infallibility under specific conditions before being interrupted by the Franco-Prussian War.
strings.timeline.councils.vatican2.title: Second Vatican Council
strings.timeline.councils.vatican2.body: The most recent ecumenical council, reshaping the Church's liturgy and relationship with the modern world.
strings.sec.swiss_guard.title: The Swiss Guard
strings.sec.swiss_guard.summary: The pope's bodyguard since 1506 — the smallest and one of the oldest standing armies in the world.
strings.sec.papal_states.title: The Papal States
strings.sec.papal_states.summary: For over a thousand years the popes were kings as well — rulers of a band of central Italy.
strings.sec.diplomacy.title: Vatican Diplomacy
strings.sec.diplomacy.summary: Nuncios, concordats and a seat at the UN — one of the oldest diplomatic services on earth.
strings.sec.insignia.title: Titles & Insignia
strings.sec.insignia.summary: The keys, the ring, the white cassock, and why a pope takes a new name.

strings.sec.jubilee.summary: The Jubilee tradition, the Holy Door, and the pilgrimage that returns every twenty-five years.
strings.fact.swiss_guard.title: The Swiss Guard in numbers
strings.fact.swiss_guard.founded.label: Founded
strings.fact.swiss_guard.strength.label: Strength
strings.fact.swiss_guard.motto.label: Motto
strings.fact.swiss_guard.requirements.label: To enlist
strings.fact.swiss_guard.requirements.value: Catholic, Swiss, unmarried men aged 19–30, at least 174 cm tall, who have completed Swiss army basic training
strings.fact.swiss_guard.oath_day.label: Oath day
strings.fact.swiss_guard.oath_day.footnote: The date marks the Sack of Rome in 1527, when the Guard died almost to a man defending Clement VII.
strings.art.swiss_guard.title: The Pontifical Swiss Guard
strings.art.swiss_guard.lead: A hundred or so men in Renaissance stripes are not a museum troupe. They are a working army, and the last of the papal military corps.
strings.art.swiss_guard.p1: Pope Julius II recruited the first company of Swiss mercenaries in 1506. Swiss soldiers were then the most sought-after in Europe — disciplined, loyal, and famously willing to die where they were told to stand. They marched into Rome on 22 January that year, the date the Guard still counts as its founding.
strings.art.swiss_guard.p2: The Guard is charged with the personal safety of the pope, and with guarding the entrances to Vatican City and the Apostolic Palace. Behind the ceremonial halberds and armour, guards are trained in unarmed combat, marksmanship and close protection, and work closely with the Vatican Gendarmerie.
strings.art.swiss_guard.p3: On 6 May 1527 the mutinous army of Emperor Charles V stormed Rome. Of the 189 guards on duty, 147 were killed holding the enemy at the steps of St Peter's while a small detachment led Pope Clement VII to safety through the Passetto, the raised corridor to Castel Sant'Angelo. New recruits are still sworn in on 6 May, in memory of that stand.
strings.art.swiss_guard.callout.title: Not designed by Michelangelo
strings.art.swiss_guard.callout.body: The blue, red and yellow striped uniform is often credited to Michelangelo or Raphael. In fact its modern form was designed by Commandant Jules Repond around 1914; the colours are those of the Medici and della Rovere popes.
strings.art.swiss_guard.p4: Entry requirements are unusually specific, and have changed little in centuries:
strings.art.swiss_guard.li_swiss: A citizen of Switzerland who has completed basic training with the Swiss Armed Forces.
strings.art.swiss_guard.li_catholic: A practising Catholic man of good character, with a certificate of good conduct.
strings.art.swiss_guard.li_age: Aged between 19 and 30 at entry, and at least 174 centimetres tall.
strings.art.swiss_guard.li_training: Unmarried on entry; a guard may later marry with permission, after a minimum term of service.
strings.art.swiss_guard.p5: The famous striped uniform is worn for ceremonies and guard duty at the gates; a plainer blue version is used for everyday work. The gala dress is completed by a steel morion helmet, worn with a plume whose colour marks rank.
strings.art.papal_states.title: When the Pope Was a King
strings.art.papal_states.lead: For eleven centuries the successors of Peter governed real territory, levied taxes and went to war. The loss of it made the modern papacy.
strings.art.papal_states.p1: The Papal States were a swathe of central Italy — at their height reaching from Rome across to the Adriatic — ruled directly by the pope as a temporal sovereign. Their existence shaped, and often complicated, the Church's spiritual mission for more than a thousand years.
strings.art.papal_states.p2: The turning point came in 756, when the Frankish king Pepin the Short defeated the Lombards and handed the conquered lands not to the emperor in Constantinople but to the pope. This Donation of Pepin gave the papacy a territorial state that would last, in one form or another, until 1870.
strings.art.papal_states.p3: Later medieval claims leaned on the Donation of Constantine, a document purporting to show that the emperor Constantine had granted the popes authority over Rome and the West. In the fifteenth century the scholar Lorenzo Valla proved it a forgery — but by then the Papal States were long established in fact.
strings.art.papal_states.callout.title: A double role
strings.art.papal_states.callout.body: Ruling a state gave the popes independence from other kings, but it also entangled them in wars, taxation and dynastic politics — the very things reformers most often held against them.
strings.art.papal_states.p4: The nineteenth century swept them away. Napoleon annexed the territory; the Congress of Vienna restored it in 1815; then the movement for Italian unification absorbed it piece by piece. When Italian troops entered Rome in 1870, the Papal States ceased to exist, and the pope withdrew inside the Vatican — a stalemate not resolved until the Lateran Treaty of 1929.
strings.tl.papal_states.title: The Papal States, 756–1870
strings.tl.ps.756.title: The Donation of Pepin
strings.tl.ps.756.body: The Frankish king Pepin the Short gives the papacy the lands taken from the Lombards, creating a papal state in central Italy.
strings.tl.ps.1309.title: The Avignon papacy
strings.tl.ps.1309.body: For nearly seventy years the popes reside at Avignon in France, and the Papal States fall into disorder and near-anarchy.
strings.tl.ps.1798.title: The Roman Republic
strings.tl.ps.1798.body: French revolutionary armies invade, proclaim a Roman Republic and carry Pius VI off into captivity, where he dies.
strings.tl.ps.1815.title: Restored at Vienna
strings.tl.ps.1815.body: After Napoleon's fall, the Congress of Vienna gives the Papal States back to the pope, largely in their old borders.
strings.tl.ps.1861.title: The Kingdom of Italy
strings.tl.ps.1861.body: Italian unification absorbs most of the papal territory; the new Kingdom of Italy claims Rome as its intended capital.
strings.tl.ps.1870.title: The capture of Rome
strings.tl.ps.1870.body: Italian troops breach the walls at Porta Pia on 20 September. The Papal States end, and the temporal power is gone.
strings.art.diplomacy.title: The Holy See in the World
strings.art.diplomacy.lead: The Holy See keeps ambassadors, signs treaties and sits at the United Nations — a diplomatic reach out of all proportion to its size.
strings.art.diplomacy.p1: The Holy See maintains full diplomatic relations with more than 180 states, plus the European Union and the Sovereign Military Order of Malta. Its diplomatic service is among the oldest in continuous existence anywhere, with roots in the papal legates of the early Middle Ages.
strings.art.diplomacy.p2: The pope's ambassador to a country is called a nuncio, and his embassy a nunciature. Under the 1961 Vienna Convention, in states that agree to it the nuncio is automatically the dean of the resident diplomatic corps — a courtesy going back centuries, regardless of how long he has served.
strings.art.diplomacy.p3: A concordat is a treaty between the Holy See and a state, setting out the position of the Catholic Church within that country — its schools, appointments, property and freedoms. The 1929 concordat with Italy and the 1933 agreement with Germany are among the most studied examples.
strings.art.diplomacy.p4: The Holy See has been a Permanent Observer at the United Nations since 1964. It is not a member state and does not vote, but it speaks in debates, signs conventions, and takes part in major UN conferences — a deliberate choice to keep a moral rather than a political voice.
strings.art.diplomacy.callout.title: The Holy See, not the State
strings.art.diplomacy.callout.body: All of this diplomacy is conducted by the Holy See — the governing authority of the Church — and not by Vatican City State. It is the See that other governments recognise and exchange ambassadors with.
strings.art.insignia.title: Titles, Symbols and Names
strings.art.insignia.lead: The pope answers to a stack of titles, carries a handful of ancient symbols, and almost always sets aside his own name.
strings.art.insignia.p1: No single title captures the office. The Annuario Pontificio, the Holy See's yearbook, lists several, each pointing to a different aspect of what the pope is and does.
strings.art.insignia.grid.pontiff.label: Supreme Pontiff
strings.art.insignia.grid.pontiff.value: Pontifex Maximus — "greatest bridge-builder," an ancient Roman title now meaning head of the universal Church
strings.art.insignia.grid.vicar.label: Vicar of Christ
strings.art.insignia.grid.vicar.value: One who stands in the place of Christ as shepherd of the Church on earth
strings.art.insignia.grid.bishop.label: Bishop of Rome
strings.art.insignia.grid.bishop.value: The root of every other title: the pope is first of all the bishop of the local Church of Rome
strings.art.insignia.grid.servant.label: Servant of the Servants of God
strings.art.insignia.grid.servant.value: Servus servorum Dei — a title of humility used by popes since Gregory the Great
strings.art.insignia.li_keys: The crossed keys — one gold, one silver — recall Christ's words to Peter, "I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 16:19).
strings.art.insignia.li_tiara: The tiara, or triple crown, once placed on a new pope's head. No pope has worn it since Paul VI set his aside in 1963; it still appears on the coat of arms.
strings.art.insignia.li_ring: The Ring of the Fisherman, engraved with Peter casting his net, is made anew for each pope and defaced with a chisel at his death.
strings.art.insignia.li_pallium: The pallium, a narrow woollen band worn over the shoulders, is a mark of a shepherd carrying the lost sheep.
strings.art.insignia.li_cassock: The white cassock, worn since the sixteenth century — often traced to Pius V, who kept his white Dominican habit after his election.
strings.art.insignia.p2: On accepting election, a pope is asked by what name he wishes to be called. The custom began in 533 with a priest named Mercurius, who thought it unfitting for a pope to carry the name of a pagan god and chose to reign as John II. The name a pope takes is often read as a signal of the pontificate to come.
strings.art.insignia.callout.title: The first Francis
strings.art.insignia.callout.body: In 2013 Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio chose a name no pope had used before — Francis, after Francis of Assisi — a break with more than a thousand years of reusing earlier papal names.
strings.art.jubilee.title: The Holy Year
strings.art.jubilee.lead: Every twenty-five years the Church calls a Jubilee: a year of pilgrimage, pardon and a door that is only open while it lasts.
strings.art.jubilee.p1: A Jubilee, or Holy Year, is a special year of grace in which the Church offers a fuller remission of the temporal punishment for sin, on the usual conditions of pilgrimage, confession, Communion and prayer. The idea reaches back to the jubilee year of the Book of Leviticus, a time of release and return proclaimed every fiftieth year.
strings.art.jubilee.p2: The first Christian Jubilee was proclaimed by Pope Boniface VIII in 1300, drawing enormous crowds of pilgrims to Rome. It was such a success that later popes shortened the interval, and since 1475 an ordinary Jubilee has been held every twenty-five years.
strings.art.jubilee.p3: The sign of a Jubilee is the Holy Door. At the start of the year the pope opens the Holy Door of St Peter's Basilica; the other three major basilicas of Rome open theirs too. Pilgrims pass through as a gesture of leaving the old life behind and entering grace. When the year ends, the doors are sealed shut again until the next Holy Year.
strings.art.jubilee.callout.title: Pilgrims of Hope
strings.art.jubilee.callout.body: The ordinary Jubilee of 2025 was called under the motto "Pilgrims of Hope," its Holy Door opened at Christmas 2024.
strings.art.jubilee.p4: Besides the ordinary Jubilees on the twenty-five-year cycle, a pope may proclaim an extraordinary Jubilee to mark a particular event or theme — as with the Holy Year of the Redemption in 1983 and the Jubilee of Mercy in 2015–16.
strings.tl.jubilees.title: The Holy Years
strings.tl.jub.1300.title: The first Jubilee
strings.tl.jub.1300.body: Boniface VIII proclaims the first Holy Year. Pilgrims flood Rome, and the Jubilee tradition is born.
strings.tl.jub.1475.title: Every twenty-five years
strings.tl.jub.1475.body: The interval settles at twenty-five years, so that most people might see a Jubilee at least once in a lifetime.
strings.tl.jub.1983.title: Holy Year of the Redemption
strings.tl.jub.1983.body: John Paul II calls an extraordinary Jubilee marking 1,950 years since the traditional date of the Crucifixion.
strings.tl.jub.2000.title: The Great Jubilee
strings.tl.jub.2000.body: The Jubilee of the year 2000 marks two thousand years since the birth of Christ, one of the largest pilgrimages in history.
strings.tl.jub.2015.title: The Jubilee of Mercy
strings.tl.jub.2015.body: An extraordinary Holy Year devoted to God's mercy, with Holy Doors opened in dioceses around the world, not only in Rome.
strings.tl.jub.2025.title: Pilgrims of Hope
strings.tl.jub.2025.body: The ordinary Jubilee of 2025, its Holy Door opened at Christmas 2024 under the theme of hope.
strings.sec.hierarchy.title: The Hierarchy of the Church
strings.sec.hierarchy.summary: One body, many members — the ranks from the lay faithful up to the Bishop of Rome.
strings.sec.cardinals.title: The College of Cardinals
strings.sec.cardinals.summary: The men in red who counsel the Pope and elect his successor — and their three ancient orders.
strings.stepper.hierarchy.title: The Ranks of the Church
strings.stepper.hierarchy.intro: The Church is one body with many members. These are its degrees, from the whole People of God to the Bishop of Rome who serves them all.
strings.stepper.hierarchy.laity.title: The Laity — the Faithful
strings.stepper.hierarchy.laity.body: The vast majority of the Church: all the baptized who are not ordained. Called to carry the Gospel into the world — in family, work and society — they share in Christ's priestly, prophetic and kingly mission and are the Church's presence in ordinary life.
strings.stepper.hierarchy.deacons.title: Deacons
strings.stepper.hierarchy.deacons.body: The first degree of Holy Orders, ordained for service rather than priesthood. A deacon may baptize, proclaim the Gospel and preach, assist at the altar, witness marriages and conduct funerals. 'Permanent' deacons may be married men; 'transitional' deacons are on the way to priesthood.
strings.stepper.hierarchy.priests.title: Priests
strings.stepper.hierarchy.priests.body: Ordained co-workers of the bishop, acting in the person of Christ the Head. A priest offers the Mass, forgives sins in confession, anoints the sick, and shepherds a parish. Priests are either diocesan or members of religious orders.
strings.stepper.hierarchy.bishops.title: Bishops
strings.stepper.hierarchy.bishops.body: Successors of the apostles, holding the fullness of Holy Orders. A bishop teaches, sanctifies and governs a diocese, ordains priests and deacons, and confers Confirmation. An archbishop leads a major see; the bishops together, with the Pope, form the college that governs the Church.
strings.stepper.hierarchy.cardinals.title: Cardinals
strings.stepper.hierarchy.cardinals.body: Senior churchmen, almost always bishops, chosen by the Pope as his chief counsellors. Together they form the College of Cardinals, and those under 80 elect the next pope in conclave. 'Cardinal' is not a separate order of ordination but the highest dignity below the papacy.
strings.stepper.hierarchy.pope.title: The Pope
strings.stepper.hierarchy.pope.body: The Bishop of Rome and successor of St Peter, the visible head of the whole Church. He holds supreme, full and universal authority, and is the lasting source and foundation of the Church's unity in faith and communion.
strings.art.cardinals.title: The College of Cardinals
strings.art.cardinals.lead: The men in red who advise the Pope and choose his successor — and the three ancient orders they are still divided into.
strings.art.cardinals.p1: A cardinal is a senior member of the clergy chosen by the Pope to be among his closest advisers and collaborators. The name comes from the Latin cardo, a hinge — the cardinals are the hinges on which the governance of the Church turns. Together they make up the College of Cardinals, and their most solemn task is to elect a new pope. Today almost every cardinal is already a bishop.
strings.art.cardinals.p2: Since ancient times the College has been divided into three ranks — a memory of the clergy of the city of Rome itself, where the cardinals began as its senior bishops, priests and deacons:
strings.art.cardinals.grid.bishop.label: Cardinal Bishops
strings.art.cardinals.grid.bishop.value: The highest rank — historically the bishops of the seven suburbicarian sees around Rome, and today also the Eastern Catholic patriarchs. The Dean of the College is chosen from among them.
strings.art.cardinals.grid.priest.label: Cardinal Priests
strings.art.cardinals.grid.priest.value: The most numerous rank — usually archbishops of major dioceses across the world, each assigned a titular church in Rome as a sign of their bond to the city.
strings.art.cardinals.grid.deacon.label: Cardinal Deacons
strings.art.cardinals.grid.deacon.value: Usually cardinals serving in the Roman Curia, each given a titular deaconry. The senior cardinal deacon, the protodeacon, announces “Habemus Papam” from the balcony.
strings.art.cardinals.p3: Beyond electing the pope, cardinals head the dicasteries of the Roman Curia, advise the pope gathered in consistory, and help govern the Church during a sede vacante, when the papal see is empty. A new cardinal is created by the pope in a public ceremony and receives the scarlet biretta and zucchetto — the “red hat” — whose colour signifies his readiness to shed his blood for the faith.
strings.art.cardinals.callout.title: Why under eighty?
strings.art.cardinals.callout.body: Since 1970 only cardinals who have not reached the age of 80 on the day the see falls vacant may enter the conclave and vote. The number of these cardinal electors is normally capped at 120.
strings.hierarchy.carousel.label: Six roles — swipe to explore
strings.cardinals.carousel.label: Three orders — swipe to explore
strings.art.cardinals.orders.note: Cardinal bishop, priest and deacon are orders within the College of Cardinals, not additional degrees of the sacrament of Holy Orders. The shields shown here are illustrative learning emblems, not universal official coats of arms.
strings.sec.canonisation.title: Steps to Sainthood
strings.sec.canonisation.summary: How the Church investigates a holy life and declares a saint — the four stages from Servant of God to canonisation.
strings.stepper.canonisation.title: How a Saint Is Made
strings.stepper.canonisation.intro: The Church does not so much make saints as recognise them. A cause moves through four stages, each demanding careful proof, and can take decades or even centuries.
strings.stepper.canonisation.step1.title: Servant of God
strings.stepper.canonisation.step1.body: A cause may open at least five years after death (the pope can waive the wait). The local bishop, with Rome's nihil obstat, opens an investigation into the person's life, writings and reputation for holiness. From this point they are called a Servant of God.
strings.stepper.canonisation.step2.title: Venerable — Heroic Virtue
strings.stepper.canonisation.step2.body: The evidence is gathered into a formal study, the positio, and examined by the Dicastery for the Causes of Saints. If the pope confirms that the person lived the virtues to a heroic degree — or died a martyr — they are declared Venerable.
strings.stepper.canonisation.step3.title: Blessed — Beatification
strings.stepper.canonisation.step3.body: One miracle worked through the candidate's intercession must be proven — usually a medically inexplicable healing — and rigorously verified by doctors and theologians. The pope then beatifies the Venerable, who is called Blessed and may be venerated locally. Martyrs may be beatified without a miracle.
strings.stepper.canonisation.step4.title: Saint — Canonisation
strings.stepper.canonisation.step4.body: A second miracle, occurring after beatification, must be verified. The pope then solemnly canonises the Blessed, declaring them a Saint of the universal Church — worthy of public veneration everywhere, with a feast day and churches dedicated in their name.
